newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU blames budget fraud on organised crime.
newsitem.headline: EU blames budget fraud on organised crime.

text.p: Mafia-style crime was behind a major part of detected fraud against the European Union's budget in 1996, which rose to 1.3 billion Ecus ($1.47 billion), the European Commission said on Tuesday.
"International organised crime accounts for a lot of losses in the Community budget," said EU Anti-Fraud Commissioner Anita Gradin, presenting the Commission's annual fraud report.
"These gangs not only defraud the EU. They are often engaged in other types of crime such as trafficking in human beings, drug smuggling, car theft and money laundering," she said.
Last year, 4,500 cases of fraud and irregularities were reported, affecting especially Germany and Italy. Less than five percent of the cases accounted for more than half the money involved.
"This clearly shows that well-organised international crime syndicates are responsible for a large proportion of the losses of EU money," Gradin said.
But there had also been improvements in the 15-nation bloc's fight against fraud and more effective detection.

"I know that the increasing figures for reported fraud and irregularities are a result of the huge efforts we have put into reorganising and improving the Commission's anti-fraud measures," Gradin said.
"We've been able to step up the measures available to us in this area," she told a press conference, adding that EU efforts were targeted on major international fraud operations.
The EU executive on Tuesday also adopted a work programme for the fight against fraud in 1997/98, continuing a strategy launched in 1994 to step up the fight against fraudsters.

Fraud and irregularities affecting budget spending and revenue detected by member states and the European Commission cost the EU and its member states 1.3 billion Ecus last year compared to 1.1 billion in 1995.

Examples of large scale fraud listed in the report involved cigarette smuggling, olive oil exports, payments of value added tax and regional support as well as beef exports and imports of canned tuna and much else.
"In 1996 the smuggling of cigarettes for the purpose of fraudulent sales in the Community again emerged as the chief activity of crime syndicates," the Commission's report said.
Organised fraud had increased dramaticially on the revenue side of the EU budget and irregularities with customs and levies amounted to 787 million Ecus compared with 717 million in 1995.
Almost half of the total detected cases concerned EU farm spending, which accounts for roughly half of the bloc's total budget of 82 billion Ecus.
Despite recent agriculture reforms, detected fraud and irregularities in market support and export refunds rose.

"The big fraudsters take advantage of the system of market support and export refunds," the report said. "The largest sums are lost on irregularities involving cereals, beef, olive oil, fruits and vegetables."
"Recovery by member states of money has been extremely slow and cumbersome," it said.

Even if the Europen Commission's tools for fighting fraud had improved considerably, Gradin said there was a need to further improve detection, recovery of embezzled money and to prepare for the enlargement of the EU.
"The Union has started to create a legal framework to protect its money and to ensure that criminals are punished," she said. "But still more has to be done to secure our taxpayers' money."
